def: Address binding maps a program's logical (virtual) addresses to physical memory addresses, and the MMU is the hardware that performs this translation at run time using a relocation/base register.
exp: A program's addresses go through three possible binding stages. Compile-time binding fixes physical addresses when the compiler runs, which only works if the process is guaranteed to load at a known fixed location — impractical for multiprogramming. Load-time binding fixes addresses when the program is loaded into memory, allowing relocation but not movement afterward. Execution-time (dynamic) binding defers translation until each memory reference, using hardware support — this is what modern systems use, because it lets a process be moved (swapped, compacted) after execution starts. The CPU generates logical (virtual) addresses; the Memory Management Unit (MMU) translates each one into a physical address before the memory bus sees it. The simplest MMU scheme uses a base (relocation) register, added to every logical address, and a limit register, checked against the logical address to catch out-of-bounds access before translation — a process can never see or touch another process's memory. Logical address space is everything a process can name; physical address space is the actual RAM. The distinction is what makes protection and relocation possible at all: the CPU only ever computes with addresses relative to 0, and hardware fills in the rest.
facts: Logical address = address generated by CPU; physical address = actual address seen by memory unit.
MMU adds the base (relocation) register value to every logical address to form the physical address.
Limit register bounds the logical address; exceeding it raises a protection trap before translation completes.
Execution-time binding is the only scheme that supports moving a process during execution (needs hardware MMU support).
Compile-time and load-time binding produce logical address = physical address (no runtime translation).
traps: Compile-time binding is not 'faster because no MMU' — it's simply infeasible once multiple processes share memory, since the address is baked in before the loader even runs.

Do not confuse the limit register (bounds check) with the base register (relocation offset) — a question may ask which register catches an out-of-bounds access (limit), not which one translates the address (base).
Logical and physical address spaces being 'the same' is true only under compile-time/load-time binding, not the general case — a question testing execution-time binding expects them to differ.

def: The resident monitor is the permanently memory-resident part of early batch operating systems that loads and sequences user jobs on a single-program 'base machine', protected from user programs by base and bounds (limit) registers.
exp: The 'base machine' is the bare hardware with a CPU, memory, and I/O — no built-in protection or multiprogramming. Early batch systems added a resident monitor: a small piece of software kept permanently in one region of memory (traditionally the low end) that reads jobs from an input device, loads the next job into the remaining memory, transfers control, and reclaims control at job end. Because only one job ran at a time, this needed no address translation, only protection: a fence or bounds register marked the boundary between monitor and user area, and any user instruction addressing memory below the fence trapped to the monitor. Two-register base/bounds schemes generalized this: the base register gives the start of the user's allocated region, the bounds (limit) register gives its size, and hardware checks every address against bounds before adding base — the same base/limit idea used in later contiguous-allocation and paging systems. Multiple base registers extend the idea by giving a process several independently relocatable, independently bounded regions (for example, one base/limit pair for code, one for data, one for stack) instead of a single flat region — an early step toward segmentation, since each region can be relocated and protected on its own.
facts: Resident monitor = permanently memory-resident supervisor in early batch systems; runs one job at a time.
The base machine has no protection hardware; the monitor's own protection depends on the fence/bounds register.
Base/bounds (base/limit) is a two-register scheme: base = start of region, limit = size, checked before every access.
Multiple base registers give one process several relocatable regions (e.g. code, data, stack) instead of one.
A user program addressing below the fence or beyond bounds traps to the monitor/OS rather than corrupting it.
traps: The resident monitor era had no multiprogramming — one job at a time — so don't attribute partitioning or scheduling algorithms to it; that comes with multiprogramming with fixed/variable partitions.
Base/bounds registers alone give protection and relocation but not fine-grained sharing between processes — that needs segmentation or paging with permission bits.
'Multiple base registers' is often confused with paging's per-page mapping — multiple base registers give a handful of large, programmer-defined regions, not many small fixed-size pages.

def: Multiprogramming with fixed partitions divides memory into a small number of partitions of predetermined (possibly unequal) size, each holding at most one process, wasting the unused tail of a partition as internal fragmentation.
exp: In this scheme, physical memory is divided at system-generation time into a fixed number of partitions, each of a fixed size (sizes may differ from partition to partition, but each is chosen once and stays constant thereafter). A process is loaded into the smallest partition large enough to hold it, using either separate ready queues per partition size or one queue scanned for the best fit among free partitions. Because a partition's size is fixed but a process rarely matches it exactly, the leftover space inside the partition — between the end of the process and the end of the partition — is wasted; this is internal fragmentation, since the waste is internal to an allocated region, not visible as a separate free block. Example: a 500 KB partition holding a 350 KB process wastes 150 KB that no other process can use, even though the OS knows that space is idle. The number of partitions also fixes the maximum degree of multiprogramming, and a process bigger than the largest partition simply cannot run. This is the earliest true multiprogramming memory scheme, historically associated with OS/360's MFT (Multiprogramming with a Fixed number of Tasks).
facts: Partition sizes and count are fixed at system generation/boot time, not changed while the system runs.
Internal fragmentation = partition size minus process size; wasted space is unusable by any other process.
Degree of multiprogramming is capped by the number of partitions.
A process larger than every partition cannot be loaded at all under this scheme.
Historically known as MFT (Multiprogramming with a Fixed number of Tasks) in IBM OS/360.
traps: Fixed partitions produce internal fragmentation (waste inside an allocated block); variable partitions produce external fragmentation (waste in unallocated gaps) — MCQs swap these terms as distractors.
'Fixed' refers to partition boundaries being fixed, not that all partitions are the same size — unequal-size fixed partitions are still 'fixed partitioning'.

Best-fit/first-fit/worst-fit placement strategies are associated with variable partitioning, not fixed partitioning, since fixed partitions have no placement choice beyond which same-sized region to use.
mnem: Fixed partition -> fixed boundary -> waste stays INside -> INternal fragmentation.

def: Multiprogramming with variable partitions allocates each process a memory hole exactly as large as it needs, eliminating internal fragmentation but scattering unusable small gaps across memory as external fragmentation, which compaction removes by sliding processes together.
exp: Here memory is not pre-divided; the OS tracks a list of free holes and, when a process arrives, allocates a hole exactly (or approximately) its size, splitting the hole into an allocated part and a smaller free remainder. This removes internal fragmentation (the process gets exactly what it needs) but as processes come and go, memory breaks into many small, scattered holes too small individually for any waiting process — external fragmentation — even though total free space may be large. Three classic placement strategies search the hole list: first-fit stops at the first hole big enough (fastest); best-fit scans all holes and picks the smallest one that fits (minimises leftover in that hole, but tends to leave many tiny unusable slivers, and is slower since it must scan everything); worst-fit picks the largest hole (leaves the biggest, most reusable leftover, but empirically fragments badly too and is also a full scan). Analysis shows first-fit and best-fit both waste, on average, about one-third of memory to fragmentation (the 'fifty-percent rule': for N allocated blocks, about 0.5N further blocks are lost to fragmentation). Compaction fixes external fragmentation by relocating processes to make free space contiguous, but requires all processes to be relocatable (execution-time binding) and costs time proportional to the data shuffled.
facts: Variable partitioning has zero internal fragmentation but is prone to external fragmentation.
First-fit: stop at first hole >= request size; fastest on average.
Best-fit: scan all holes, choose the smallest that fits; minimizes leftover but tends to create many tiny unusable slivers and is slower.
Worst-fit: scan all holes, choose the largest; leaves a big, more usable leftover but performs worst empirically.
Fifty-percent rule: statistical analysis shows first-fit/best-fit lose about 1/3 of memory to fragmentation.
Compaction requires execution-time (dynamic) address binding since it physically moves running processes.
traps: Best-fit is NOT the best-performing strategy in practice, despite the name — it tends to leave the most unusably small fragments; first-fit is generally faster and no worse in fragmentation.
Worst-fit is motivated by leaving large, reusable remainders, not by being 'the worst choice' — but empirical studies still rank it behind first-fit/best-fit overall.
Internal vs external fragmentation is the most tested confusion here: fixed partitions -> internal; variable partitions -> external.
Compaction is only possible if addresses are bound at execution time (dynamic relocation) — a system using compile/load-time binding cannot compact.

def: Paging divides logical memory into fixed-size pages and physical memory into same-size frames, and maps each page to any free frame via a per-process page table, eliminating external fragmentation entirely.
exp: Physical memory is cut into fixed-size frames and logical memory into same-size pages (frame size = page size, both a power of two, say 2^n bytes). A logical address is not translated by adding a single base value; instead it is split by the hardware into two fields: a page number p (the high-order bits) and a page offset d (the low-order n bits) — the offset never changes during translation because it locates a byte within a page/frame, which is the same size on both sides. The page number indexes the process's page table, a per-process array giving the frame number f currently holding that page; the physical address is then f concatenated with d (equivalently f x 2^n + d). Worked example: page size 1 KB (2^10, so n = 10 offset bits), logical address 5000. Offset = 5000 mod 1024 = 904, page number = 5000 div 1024 = 4. If the page table says page 4 -> frame 7, the physical address = 7 x 1024 + 904 = 8072. Because any page can sit in any free frame, and frames are allocated one at a time, paging leaves no external fragmentation — only a small amount of internal fragmentation in the last, partially-used page of a process.
facts: Page size = frame size, always a power of two, chosen so the offset is just the low-order bits.
Logical address splits into (page number p, offset d); p indexes the page table, d passes through unchanged.
Physical address = frame_number x page_size + offset.
Paging eliminates external fragmentation but can leave internal fragmentation in the last page of a process (average half a page per process).
Each process has its own page table; the page table itself lives in memory (or partly in fast hardware — see TLB).
traps: Paging removes external fragmentation, not internal — the last page of a process is usually only partly used, which is internal fragmentation; questions swap the two.
The offset bits are NOT translated/looked up — only the page number goes through the page table; a common error is to assume the whole address is translated.
Page size must be a power of two so page number/offset can be split by simple bit-shifting rather than division — real systems never use arbitrary page sizes.
Contiguous physical placement is not required for a process under paging — pages can (and usually do) sit in non-adjacent frames; only the page table's mapping matters.
mnem: p page number picks the row, d displacement stays put.
rel: Demand paging and page fault handling

sub: TLB, effective access time, page tables
def: The Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) is a small, fast associative hardware cache of recent page-table entries that avoids a second memory access on every address translation; multilevel and inverted page tables keep the page table itself from becoming too large.
exp: Every plain paged translation costs two memory accesses: one to read the page table entry, one for the actual data. The TLB is a small associative (content-addressable) cache holding recent (page number -> frame number) pairs; on a hit, translation is essentially free, on a miss the page table must still be consulted (and the TLB updated). Effective access time (EAT) worked example: TLB access time = 20 ns, memory access = 100 ns, hit ratio = 80%. EAT = 0.8 x (20 + 100) + 0.2 x (20 + 100 + 100) = 0.8 x 120 + 0.2 x 220 = 96 + 44 = 140 ns — well below the 200 ns a system with no TLB would always pay. For large address spaces a single flat page table would itself be huge (and mostly unused), so multilevel (hierarchical) paging pages the page table itself, adding one extra memory access per level but only allocating the levels actually used. An inverted page table instead keeps one entry per physical frame (not per logical page), indexed by frame and storing which (process, page) owns it — its size is tied to physical memory, not to the much larger virtual address space, but lookup requires searching by content, usually sped up with a hash table.
facts: TLB = associative cache of (page, frame) pairs; hit avoids the extra page-table memory access.
EAT with TLB = hit_ratio x (TLB+mem time) + miss_ratio x (TLB+mem+mem time).
Multilevel page tables add one memory access per extra level but avoid allocating unused page-table space.
Inverted page table size is proportional to physical memory size, not virtual address space size.
Inverted page tables need a search (often hash-assisted) by (pid, page) since they're indexed by frame, not page number.
traps: A TLB miss does not mean a page fault — it just means the page table (in memory) must be consulted; the page may still be resident.
EAT formulas are a common numeric-trap MCQ: forgetting to add the TLB access time itself to both the hit and miss branches understates the answer.
Inverted page tables save memory but cost lookup speed — don't assume a smaller structure automatically means faster access.
Multilevel paging trades table-space savings for extra memory references per translation — more levels is not free.

def: Segmentation divides a program into logically meaningful, variable-sized units (code, stack, heap, each a segment) described by a segment table of base and limit pairs, giving the programmer's view of memory rather than paging's arbitrary fixed-size slices.
exp: A segment is a logically meaningful, variable-length unit of a program — its code, its stack, a particular array or module — as opposed to a page, which is a fixed-size slice with no relation to program structure. A logical address is (segment number s, offset d); the segment table gives each segment's base (starting physical address) and limit (length); the offset is checked against the limit (protection) and then added to the base to form the physical address, much like a base/bounds pair but one per segment instead of one per process. Because segmentation exposes the program's own logical divisions, it naturally supports per-segment protection (e.g., code segments read/execute-only) and controlled sharing (two processes can share one code segment via matching segment-table entries) in a way flat paging cannot express directly. The cost is that segments, being variable-sized, suffer external fragmentation exactly like variable-partition allocation. Paged segmentation combines both: each segment is itself divided into fixed-size pages, so a segment table entry points not to a base address but to a page table for that segment — this removes external fragmentation while keeping segmentation's logical structure and protection/sharing granularity. Systems like Multics and the x86 architecture historically used variants of paged segmentation.
facts: Segment table entry = (base, limit); logical address = (segment number, offset), offset checked against limit before adding base.
Segmentation matches the programmer's/compiler's logical view (code, stack, data); paging is purely physical bookkeeping, invisible to the program.
Pure segmentation suffers external fragmentation (like variable partitions); pure paging suffers (small) internal fragmentation only.
Paged segmentation pages each segment to remove external fragmentation while keeping per-segment protection and sharing.
Segmentation naturally supports fine-grained protection/sharing per logical unit; paging needs extra bits/structures to approximate this.
traps: 'Segmentation has external fragmentation, paging has internal fragmentation' is the single most tested contrast in this topic — don't invert it.
Segments are variable length; pages are fixed length — a question describing 'fixed-size units visible to the programmer' is describing neither correctly.

Paged segmentation is not the same as multilevel paging — paged segmentation's outer table is indexed by logically meaningful segment number, a multilevel page table's outer table is just an arbitrary split of a flat page number.

def: Virtual memory lets a process execute with an address space larger than physical memory actually installed, by keeping only the actively used portion resident and fetching the rest from disk on demand — practical because real programs exhibit locality of reference.
exp: Virtual memory is the illusion, given to each process, of a large, contiguous private address space, independent of how much physical RAM the machine actually has and independent of what other processes are doing. It finally separates logical address space from physical address space completely: a process's virtual address space can exceed total installed RAM, because at any instant only a fraction of it needs to be physically resident. This works in practice — rather than being a dangerous trick — because of locality of reference: programs spend extended periods accessing a small, slowly-changing subset of their code and data (loops, currently-called functions, a working data set), both in time (temporal locality: recently used items are likely reused soon) and space (spatial locality: items near a recently used address are likely used soon too). Because of locality, keeping only that active subset in memory and fetching the rest only when actually referenced (demand paging) wastes little time on misses while saving large amounts of RAM. Benefits include: programs larger than physical memory can run at all, more processes fit into RAM simultaneously (higher degree of multiprogramming since each needs less resident memory), and process start-up is faster since the whole program need not be loaded before execution begins.
facts: Virtual memory fully decouples logical (virtual) address space size from physical RAM size.
Its practicality rests on locality of reference: temporal (reuse soon) and spatial (nearby addresses used soon).
Benefits: programs can exceed physical RAM, higher degree of multiprogramming, faster process start.
Virtual memory is most commonly implemented via demand paging; demand segmentation is a rarer alternative.
Without locality, virtual memory would thrash constantly, since almost every reference would need a fresh fetch from disk.
traps: Virtual memory is not the same as swap space/disk space alone — swap is the backing store mechanism, virtual memory is the addressing concept it supports.

Virtual memory does not make programs run faster than if fully resident — it trades some page-fault overhead for the ability to run at all or fit more processes; assuming it's a pure speed win is wrong.
The justification for virtual memory is locality of reference, not 'disks got cheap' — a question asking why demand paging works acceptably wants locality, not cost.
rel: Demand paging and page fault handling

sub: Demand paging and page fault handling
def: Demand paging loads a page into memory only when it is actually referenced and not already present, marking not-yet-loaded pages invalid in the page table so that a reference to one triggers a page fault trap handled by the operating system.
exp: Instead of loading an entire process into memory before it runs, demand paging loads a page only at the moment it is first referenced. Each page table entry carries a valid/invalid bit; pages not yet in memory are marked invalid. When the CPU generates an address on an invalid page, hardware traps to the OS as a page fault, and the OS runs a fixed service sequence: (1) check an internal table to confirm this was a legitimate reference to a page that simply isn't resident, not an illegal access outside the process — an illegal reference aborts the process; (2) find a free frame (or select a victim and evict it via a replacement algorithm); (3) schedule a disk read to bring the required page into that frame; (4) while waiting, the process is blocked and the CPU is given to another process; (5) once the read completes, update the page table entry with the new frame number and set the bit to valid; (6) restart the instruction that faulted, from the beginning, since the fault happened before the instruction could complete. Pure demand paging takes this to its extreme: not even the first page is preloaded, so the very first instruction fetch of a newly started process faults.
facts: Valid/invalid bit in the page table entry marks whether a page is currently resident in a frame.
Page fault service sequence: trap -> validate reference -> get free/victim frame -> disk read -> update page table -> restart instruction.
An invalid reference to memory truly outside the process (not just not-yet-loaded) causes the process to abort, not a normal page fault service.
The faulting instruction is restarted from its beginning after the fault is serviced, not resumed mid-instruction.
Pure demand paging never prefetches — even the first page faults in on first reference.
traps: A page fault is not an error/crash by default — it is a normal, expected event in demand paging; only an illegal address (outside the process's valid space) causes abnormal termination.

Restarting 'the instruction' after a fault, not just the memory access, matters for instructions with multiple operands/side effects (e.g. block move/string instructions needing special handling) — a classic exam distinction.
'Pure' demand paging specifically means zero pages are preloaded, including page 0 — a description saying 'the first page is loaded at start' is anticipatory paging, not pure demand paging.

def: Demand paging performance is measured by the effective access time (EAT), which blends the normal memory access time with the much larger page fault service time, weighted by the page fault rate p.
exp: Effective access time under demand paging is EAT = (1 - p) x ma + p x fault_service_time, where p is the page fault rate (fraction of references that fault) and ma is normal memory access time. Fault service time is dominated by disk I/O — seek, rotational latency, transfer, plus OS overhead — typically measured in milliseconds, roughly a million times slower than a memory access measured in nanoseconds. Worked example: ma = 200 ns, page fault service time = 8 ms = 8,000,000 ns, p = 0.001 (one fault per thousand references). EAT = 0.999 x 200 + 0.001 x 8,000,000 = 199.8 + 8000 = 8199.8 ns — over 40 times slower than pure memory access, from a fault rate of just 0.1%. This is why demand-paged systems are so sensitive to p: because fault_service_time is roughly 10^5-10^6 times ma, even a small p dominates the whole formula, and to keep the slowdown to, say, 10%, p typically needs to be on the order of 10^-7 or smaller for realistic numbers. Keeping p that low in practice needs enough allocated frames and a good page-replacement algorithm — this is the direct link between this performance formula and why replacement policy quality matters so much.
facts: EAT = (1-p) x memory_access_time + p x page_fault_service_time.
Page fault service time (ms range) vastly exceeds memory access time (ns range), often by 10^5-10^6x.
A tiny page fault rate can dominate EAT because of this huge time disparity — the formula is extremely sensitive to p.
Worked example: ma=200ns, service=8ms, p=0.001 gives EAT approx 8199.8ns (~41x slower than no-fault access).
Keeping the system usably fast requires p to be kept very small, motivating good frame allocation and replacement policy.
traps: A common arithmetic slip: forgetting to convert page fault service time to the same unit (ns) as memory access time before combining terms — always convert ms to ns (x10^6) first.
Do not drop the (1-p) factor on the memory-access term — even though p is tiny, at typical exam values the (1-p) term still matters to several significant figures.
A larger fault_service_time does not mean paging is a bad idea overall — it means the system must minimize p (frames, replacement algorithm, locality), not that demand paging itself is flawed.
rel: Demand paging and page fault handling

def: FIFO page replacement evicts the page that has been in memory the longest, regardless of how recently or often it was used, and is the only classical replacement algorithm that can suffer Belady's anomaly — more frames producing more page faults.
exp: FIFO tracks pages in the order they entered memory, in a simple queue; on a fault with no free frame, it evicts the oldest resident page, irrespective of how heavily that page is still being used. Worked on the reference string 7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4,2,3,0,3,2,1,2,0,1,7,0,1 with 3 frames: FIFO produces 15 page faults (trace: 7,0,1 fault filling empty frames; 2 evicts 7; 0 hits; 3 evicts 0; 0 evicts 1; 4 evicts 2; 2 evicts 3; 3 evicts 0; 0 evicts 4; 3,2 hit; 1 evicts 2; 2 evicts 3; 0,1 hit; 7 evicts 0; 0 evicts 1; 1 evicts 2 — 15 faults total). FIFO's defect is Belady's anomaly: adding more frames can, counter-intuitively, increase the fault count instead of decreasing or holding it steady. Classic demonstration: reference string 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5 gives FIFO exactly 9 faults with 3 frames but 10 faults with 4 frames — strictly worse with more memory. This anomaly is possible because FIFO's eviction order depends only on arrival time, not on future or recent use, so the queue's contents at fault-time can differ non-monotonically as frame count changes. It is the reason 'stack algorithms' (OPT, LRU) were formalized — they provably cannot exhibit this anomaly.
facts: FIFO evicts the resident page that arrived earliest, ignoring usage frequency/recency entirely.
On the reference string 7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4,2,3,0,3,2,1,2,0,1,7,0,1 with 3 frames, FIFO gives 15 page faults.
Belady's anomaly: increasing the number of frames can increase the page fault count under FIFO.
Classic anomaly demonstration: string 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5 gives FIFO 9 faults at 3 frames but 10 faults at 4 frames.
FIFO is not a 'stack algorithm' — the set of pages held with k frames is not guaranteed to be a subset of the set held with k+1 frames, which is why the anomaly is possible.
traps: Belady's anomaly is specific to FIFO among the classic algorithms — LRU and OPT are stack algorithms and are proven immune to it; an MCQ claiming LRU can suffer Belady's anomaly is false.
The anomaly is a possibility, not a guarantee — most reference strings do not trigger it under FIFO; don't assume every FIFO trace with more frames must show worse behaviour.
Do not confuse 'FIFO is simple to implement' with 'FIFO performs well' — it is cheap but frequently the worst performer of the classical algorithms, aside from the anomaly issue entirely.
mnem: FIFO: First In, First Out — and only FIFO can go 'FI-belady' with more frames.

def: Optimal (OPT) replacement evicts the page that will not be used for the longest time in the future (a theoretical best case), while LRU (Least Recently Used) evicts the page unused for the longest time in the past as a practical, implementable approximation of it.
exp: OPT looks ahead in the reference string and evicts whichever resident page will be used furthest in the future (or never again) — provably optimal, but it requires knowing the future, so it exists only as a benchmark. LRU looks backward instead: it evicts the page unused for the longest time so far, on the locality assumption that recent behaviour predicts near-future behaviour. On the same reference string as the FIFO card (7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4,2,3,0,3,2,1,2,0,1,7,0,1, 3 frames): OPT gives 9 faults, LRU gives 12, and FIFO gives 15 — the typical ordering OPT <= LRU <= FIFO. Exact LRU needs either per-page timestamps/counters (evict the minimum — costly to search) or a stack updated on every reference (most-recent page on top, victim always the bottom — cheap eviction, costly update); both need hardware help to be fast. Because true LRU is expensive, systems approximate it with second-chance (clock): frames sit in a circular list with a reference bit each; on a fault, the algorithm checks the pointed-at frame — if its bit is 1 it clears the bit and advances (a 'second chance'), if 0 it evicts that frame. Counting-based alternatives exist too: LFU evicts the least frequently used page; MFU evicts the most frequently used one (reasoning a low-count page was just brought in and hasn't had its chance). Both are used far less than LRU/clock in practice.
facts: OPT evicts the page needed furthest in the future; requires foreknowledge, so only usable as a theoretical benchmark.
LRU evicts the page unused for the longest time in the past; approximates OPT using locality.
Same reference string, 3 frames: OPT=9 faults, LRU=12 faults, FIFO=15 faults — typical ordering OPT<=LRU<=FIFO.
Exact LRU implementations: counters/timestamps (search for minimum) or a reference stack (move to top on use, victim at bottom).
Second-chance/clock approximates LRU cheaply using one reference bit per frame in a circular list.
LFU evicts the least-frequently-used page; MFU evicts the most-frequently-used page; both are counting-based and less common than LRU/clock.
traps: OPT is not implementable in a real system — it is a benchmark used only to judge how close other algorithms come, never deployed as-is.
LRU and OPT are both stack algorithms and are immune to Belady's anomaly, unlike FIFO — a question asking which of FIFO/LRU/OPT can show Belady's anomaly has exactly one correct answer, FIFO.
Second-chance (clock) is an approximation of LRU, not a different algorithm from a different family — don't treat it as unrelated to LRU in a matching question.
MFU's logic (evict the most used) is the opposite of intuition and of LFU — mixing up which one evicts high-count vs low-count pages is a common distractor.
mnem: OPT dreams of the future, LRU remembers the past, FIFO just remembers who came first.

def: Frame allocation policy decides how the fixed pool of physical frames is divided among competing processes — equally, proportionally to process size, or by priority — and whether a process may steal frames from any process (global replacement) or only from itself (local replacement).
exp: Given F usable frames and n processes, equal allocation simply gives each process F/n frames regardless of size — simple but wasteful for a small process and starving for a large one. Proportional allocation instead sizes each process's share to its virtual size: process i gets (size_i / total_size) x F frames, so bigger processes get proportionally more frames. Priority allocation weights the proportional idea by process priority/importance rather than size alone, letting the OS deliberately give high-priority processes more frames (and even let them evict frames from lower-priority processes). This connects to a second, orthogonal choice: local replacement restricts a faulting process to evicting only its own frames, so its performance is unaffected by other processes but it may be starved even with idle frames elsewhere in the system; global replacement lets any process's fault evict any frame system-wide, generally raising overall throughput but making one process's page-fault rate depend on the behaviour of unrelated processes — much less predictable, and how paging can indirectly worsen thrashing. Every process also needs a guaranteed minimum number of frames, fixed by the computer's instruction set architecture rather than choice: the worst-case number of pages a single instruction (with all its operands, plus any indirect-addressing levels) can touch at once, since an instruction cannot be restarted correctly if it can't hold all its own referenced pages simultaneously.
facts: Equal allocation: F/n frames per process, ignores process size.
Proportional allocation: frames_i = (size_i / total virtual size) x F, scaled by each process's size.
Priority allocation: weights the share (or eviction rights) by process priority rather than size alone.
Local replacement confines a process's page faults to its own allocated frames; global lets any process's frames be taken.
Minimum frames per process is fixed by the ISA: the worst-case number of pages one instruction (with operands/indirect addressing) can reference at once.
traps: Global replacement generally gives better overall system throughput than local, but at the cost of unpredictable per-process performance — a question may ask which improves throughput (global) vs which gives more predictable per-process performance (local); don't swap them.
Proportional allocation is based on process SIZE, not priority — priority allocation is the separate scheme; a question testing allocation proportional to importance wants priority allocation.

The minimum-frames number is a hardware/ISA-driven floor, not a tunable OS parameter — a question asking what determines the minimum number of frames wants instruction format/indirect addressing levels, not memory size or priority.

def: Thrashing is a collapse in CPU utilization caused by processes spending more time paging than computing because they hold too few frames for their active page set, and it is controlled by the working-set model or page-fault-frequency scheme, both of which allocate frames based on actual locality rather than a fixed count.
exp: Thrashing happens when a process (or the whole system) does not have enough frames to hold its actively-used pages, so it faults almost continuously, spends nearly all its time waiting on disk I/O rather than computing, and CPU utilization collapses. The vicious cycle: the OS, seeing low CPU utilization, assumes more processes are needed to keep the CPU busy and raises the degree of multiprogramming — but if the real cause was too few frames per process, adding processes shrinks each one's share further, worsening fault rates and utilization even more. Plotting CPU utilization against degree of multiprogramming shows utilization rising then suddenly collapsing past a threshold — that collapse is thrashing. The working-set model fixes this by tracking, for each process, WS(t, delta) — the set of distinct pages referenced in the most recent delta references (the working-set window) — and only keeps a process running if enough frames exist to cover its current working-set size; if the sum of all working-set sizes would exceed available frames, a process is suspended rather than starved. Page-fault-frequency (PFF) control is a more direct, reactive alternative: monitor each process's actual fault rate, give it more frames if the rate exceeds an upper threshold, and reclaim frames if it drops below a lower threshold — directly regulating the cause (frame count) via the symptom (fault rate).
facts: Thrashing = processes spend more time page-faulting than computing, because allocated frames are fewer than their actively used pages.
The standard trigger: OS mistakes fault-driven low CPU utilization for idle-CPU low utilization and raises multiprogramming degree, worsening the problem.
CPU utilization vs degree-of-multiprogramming graph rises then sharply collapses at the thrashing threshold.
Working set WS(t, delta) = set of distinct pages referenced in the last delta references; delta is the working-set window size.
A process is admitted/kept resident only if enough frames exist to cover its working-set size (sum of working sets <= total frames).
Page-fault-frequency (PFF) control adjusts a process's frame count directly based on whether its fault rate crosses upper/lower bounds.
traps: The fix for thrashing is NOT to add more processes to use the idle-looking CPU — that is precisely the mistake that causes/worsens thrashing; the fix is to reduce multiprogramming degree or add frames.

Working-set window size (delta) is a tunable parameter with a real trade-off: too small under-estimates locality (looks like thrashing when it isn't), too large over-estimates it (wastes frames) — don't treat delta as a fixed constant.

PFF and the working-set model solve the same problem (thrashing) via different signals — PFF reacts to fault rate directly, the working-set model reacts to the page reference set — a question may ask which is which.

def: The I/O function is organised in layers — a physical device, a device controller (the electronics that operate the device and expose registers to the CPU), and a device driver (the OS software module that knows how to talk to that specific controller) — with devices classified broadly as block or character devices.
exp: I/O organisation has three layers. The physical device is the actual hardware. The device controller is the electronics attached to it, exposing a small set of registers (data, status, control) that the CPU reads and writes to command it, either via memory-mapped I/O (registers appear at ordinary memory addresses) or dedicated I/O instructions/ports. The CPU can find out that an operation completed either by polling (repeatedly checking a status register — wastes CPU cycles) or by interrupts (the controller signals completion asynchronously, letting the CPU do other work meanwhile); bulk data transfer is typically offloaded to DMA (Direct Memory Access) hardware, which moves data directly between device and memory without the CPU copying every byte. The device driver is the OS software module written specifically for one controller type, translating the kernel's generic I/O requests into the exact register operations that controller needs, and presenting a uniform interface upward so the rest of the OS need not know device specifics. Devices are broadly classified as block devices — addressable in fixed-size blocks, support random access, seek, and are naturally cacheable/bufferable (disks, SSDs) — or character devices — an unstructured stream of bytes with no addressable position, accessed sequentially (keyboards, mice, serial ports); network devices are often treated as a distinct third case via a stream/socket abstraction.
facts: Layering: physical device -> device controller (registers) -> device driver (OS software) -> uniform kernel I/O interface.
CPU-controller communication happens via memory-mapped I/O or dedicated I/O instructions/ports.
Polling wastes CPU cycles checking status; interrupts let the CPU do other work until signalled; DMA offloads bulk data movement from the CPU entirely.
Block devices: fixed-size addressable blocks, random access, cacheable (disks/SSDs).
Character devices: unstructured byte stream, sequential access only, no seek (keyboard, mouse, serial line).
traps: DMA does not eliminate interrupts — DMA still typically interrupts the CPU once, at the end of the whole transfer, rather than once per byte/word as programmed I/O would.
A device driver is OS/kernel software, not hardware — don't confuse it with the device controller, which is the physical electronics.
Not every device fits block/character cleanly — network devices are commonly handled as a separate category (sockets/streams), a detail that trips up strict either/or questions.

def: I/O buffering holds data in memory during transfer to smooth out speed mismatches between devices and the CPU/application, ranging from a single buffer to double buffering (overlapping producer and consumer) to a circular buffer for continuous streaming, and is distinct from caching (a copy of data for reuse) and spooling (a job queue for a device usable by only one job at a time).
exp: Buffering holds in-transit data in memory to absorb the speed mismatch between a fast producer/consumer (CPU, application) and a slower device (disk, network, terminal), or vice versa. A single buffer forces strict alternation: it must be fully filled before it's consumed and fully emptied before it's refilled, so producer and consumer can never work simultaneously. Double buffering uses two buffers: while one is being filled (say, by the device), the other is being drained (by the application), and they swap roles when both finish — this overlaps I/O with computation and hides much of the device latency. A circular buffer generalises this to many slots arranged in a ring, with a producer writing at the head and a consumer reading at the tail; it suits continuous streaming I/O (audio, video, network packets) where data keeps arriving faster than a two-buffer swap could keep up cleanly. Buffering is distinct from caching — a cache holds a copy of data already fetched, purely so a future request can reuse it without re-fetching, whereas a buffer holds data only passing through once. Spooling is different again: it lets many independent jobs queue their output for a device usable by only one job at a time (the classic case being a print spooler), decoupling job completion from device availability. The kernel I/O subsystem bundles scheduling, buffering, caching, spooling, and driver interfacing behind one interface.
facts: Single buffering forces strict alternation between filling and draining; producer and consumer cannot overlap.
Double buffering overlaps production and consumption using two buffers that swap roles.
Circular (ring) buffering uses multiple slots for continuous streaming I/O without forcing pairwise swaps.
Caching keeps a reusable copy of already-fetched data; buffering holds data only in transit once.
Spooling queues output/jobs on disk for a device usable by only one job at a time (e.g., print spooler), decoupling job submission from device access.
The kernel I/O subsystem bundles scheduling, buffering, caching, spooling and driver interfacing into one abstraction.
traps: Buffering and caching are often used interchangeably in casual speech but differ in exam terms: buffering is about transit/speed-matching, caching is about reuse of already-valid data.
Spooling is not just buffering for slow devices — its defining feature is multiplexing several independent jobs onto one device that can only serve one job at a time, not just smoothing speed.

Double buffering does not eliminate wait time entirely — it only overlaps I/O with computation; if the device is much slower than consumption, the consumer still eventually stalls waiting for the next full buffer.
rel: Demand paging and page fault handling

def: Disk scheduling orders a queue of pending cylinder requests to minimize total head movement (and hence seek time), with FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK and C-LOOK trading off simplicity, fairness, and total distance travelled.
exp: Setup used throughout: cylinders 0-199, head starts at 53, pending requests (arrival order) 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67; for the directional algorithms the head moves toward higher cylinder numbers first. FCFS services requests strictly in arrival order — simple, fair, but can cause wild swings; total head movement here = 640. SSTF (Shortest Seek Time First) always jumps to the closest pending request — much better average distance (236 here) but can starve far-away requests. SCAN sweeps in one direction servicing everything in its path, continues all the way to the disk's physical end (0 or 199) even past the last request, then reverses — 331 here. LOOK is SCAN's practical refinement: it reverses as soon as the last request in that direction is serviced, without travelling to the empty boundary — 299 here, always <= SCAN's distance for the same queue. C-SCAN (circular SCAN) sweeps one direction to the physical end, then jumps back to the opposite end without servicing on the way back, and resumes the same direction — this bounds worst-case wait time more fairly than SCAN, at the cost of extra distance from the jump — 382 here. C-LOOK is C-SCAN's refinement: it jumps back only to the lowest pending request instead of the physical boundary — 322 here. Ordering here: SSTF < C-LOOK < LOOK < SCAN < C-SCAN < FCFS, though this ordering is workload-dependent, not a law.
facts: Setup: cylinders 0-199, head at 53, requests (arrival order) 98,183,37,122,14,124,65,67, sweeping toward higher numbers first.
FCFS total head movement = 640 (services strictly in arrival order).
SSTF total head movement = 236 (always services the nearest pending request; can starve distant requests).
SCAN total = 331 (sweeps to the disk's physical end even with no requests there, then reverses).
LOOK total = 299 (reverses at the last request, not the physical end — always <= SCAN's distance for the same queue).
C-SCAN total = 382 and C-LOOK total = 322 (circular versions; C-LOOK skips the empty run to the boundary that C-SCAN pays for).
traps: SCAN vs LOOK is the single most tested confusion: SCAN travels all the way to the disk boundary regardless of pending requests; LOOK stops/reverses at the last actual request. LOOK is never worse than SCAN in total distance for the same queue.
C-SCAN's return sweep is one-directional and non-servicing — it does NOT service requests on the way back to the start; only C-LOOK's jump to the nearest pending request saves the wasted run.

SSTF minimizing total seek distance does not make it the best algorithm outright — it can indefinitely starve a request far from the current cluster of activity, which SCAN/LOOK/C-SCAN/C-LOOK avoid by design.
Total head movement depends on the assumed initial direction (toward 0 vs toward the max cylinder) for SCAN/LOOK/C-SCAN/C-LOOK — always check which direction a question states before computing.
mnem: SCAN goes all the way, LOOK just looks (at the last request) and turns back.

def: A file system gives persistent named storage (the file concept, with attributes like name, size, type and permissions) plus operations (create, read, write, delete), organisation/access methods (sequential, direct, indexed), on-disk allocation strategies (contiguous, linked, indexed), free-space tracking, and directory structures that together let an OS manage disk space and let users find their files.
exp: A file is a named collection of related information persisted on secondary storage, with attributes (name, identifier, type, size, protection bits, timestamps) and standard operations (create, open, read, write, seek, delete, truncate). Access/organisation methods: sequential access reads/writes records in order only (cheapest, matches tape-era files); direct (random) access lets a program jump straight to any block by number (needed for databases); indexed access adds an index mapping keys to block addresses, giving near-direct access while still allowing sequential scans. Allocation methods place a file's blocks on disk: contiguous allocation gives fast sequential and direct access (block = start + offset) but suffers external fragmentation and can't easily grow in place; linked allocation chains each block to the next via a pointer, so no external fragmentation and easy growth, but no direct access and reliability risk if a pointer is corrupted; indexed allocation collects all block pointers into one index block, giving direct access without contiguity, at the cost of the index block itself (large files need multilevel or linked indexes). Free space is tracked via a bit vector (one bit per block), a linked list of free blocks, or grouping/counting variants. Directory structures: single-level (one shared directory, name collisions across users), two-level (one directory per user, isolates names but blocks sharing), tree-structured (arbitrary nested subdirectories), and acyclic-graph (allows shared files/subdirectories via links while forbidding true cycles, so traversal and deletion stay well-defined).
facts: File attributes: name, identifier, type, size, protection, timestamps; operations: create, open, read, write, seek, delete, truncate.
Sequential access = in-order only; direct/random access = jump to any block by number; indexed access = a key-to-block index enables near-direct access.
Contiguous allocation: fast sequential+direct access, but external fragmentation and hard in-place growth.
Linked allocation: no external fragmentation, easy growth, but no direct access and pointer-corruption risk.
Indexed allocation: direct access without contiguity, using an index block (large files may need multilevel/linked indexes).
Free space tracked via bit vector, linked free list, or grouping/counting schemes.
Directory structures: single-level, two-level, tree-structured, and acyclic-graph (shared links, no true cycles).
traps: Contiguous allocation supports BOTH sequential and direct access equally well — a common wrong answer claims only linked/indexed allocation supports direct access, when actually contiguous does too (external fragmentation is its weakness, not access mode).
Linked allocation cannot do direct/random access efficiently — to reach block n you must traverse n pointers from the start; no fragmentation does not mean no cost.

Acyclic-graph directories allow a file to be reached via multiple paths (shared subdirectories/hard links) but still forbid true cycles — allowing cycles would break simple reference-counting deletion and traversal, which is why it's acyclic, not a general graph.

A bit vector (bitmap) is simple but must be scanned to find a free block, and can itself become large for big disks — don't assume it's automatically the most efficient free-space method for every case.

Two-level directories solve the naming-collision problem of single-level directories but reintroduce a new problem: no natural way to share files across users, which tree/acyclic-graph structures address via subdirectories/links.
